sentences.text: The known fossil material of Sphenosuchus consists mainly of a well-preserved skull, with only some forelimb elements and isolated hind limb parts found.
This animal reached a total body length of 1.4 meters, making it one of the largest early crocodylomorphs.
Its lower jaw held roughly fourteen teeth, with about one-third of them being larger than the rest.
While likely a quadruped, Sphenosuchus may have been capable of facultative bipedalism.
The skull of Sphenosuchus is similar to that of crocodiles but is slightly deeper.
In Sphenosuchus, the primary head of the quadrate bone meets the prootic and squamosal bones.
The jugal bone in Sphenosuchus is large, forming the entire lower orbital margin and almost the whole of the lower temporal bar.
The parietal bone in Sphenosuchus forms nearly the entire intertemporal region and the majority of the occiput.
There is no parietal foramen present in the skull of Sphenosuchus.
Evidence from a forelimb suggests Sphenosuchus had a carpus with elongated radius and ulna bones that were metacarpal-like in structure.
In Sphenosuchus, metatarsal I is reduced, metatarsals II and IV are symmetrical, and metatarsal III is the longest.
The posttemporal fenestrae in Sphenosuchus are relatively small compared to other early archosaurs, despite size variation among the group.
Sphenosuchus was first thoroughly described in 1972 by the British paleontologist Alick Walker in a paper published in the journal Nature.
In 1927, Broom believed that Sphenosuchus was a pseudosuchian closely related to the lineage leading to true crocodiles.
Sphenosuchus is considered to have been a carnivorous and cursorial animal.
Sphenosuchus acutus is the type species and the only described species within the genus Sphenosuchus.
Sphenosuchus belongs to the parent group Crocodylomorpha.
Sphenosuchus is classified within the class Reptilia.
Sphenosuchus lived during the Hettangian to Sinemurian stages, approximately 201.4 to 192.9 million years ago.
Broom suggested in 1927 that Sphenosuchus represents a pseudosuchian well along the evolutionary line leading to modern crocodiles.
In 1995, Johann Welman argued that Sphenosuchus brain case structures were too specialized to make it the sister group of birds, despite earlier hypotheses linking the two.
Johann Welman noted a difference in the eustachian system, observing that crocodiles and Sphenosuchus have a median system while birds do not.
